title: Is Leadership Training Snake Oil?
author: Dominic Salles
summary: Salles argues that training school leaders in the how of leadership is futile, and that training should focus on what leaders do. He starts from three headteachers who shaped him, each with very different styles and flaws, all running successful schools. He then cites Rob Coe's evidence review, which finds much of the leadership-style literature methodologically unreliable while identifying evidence-backed areas of focus: learning time, learning supports and management factors. He turns Coe's model into a checklist of fourteen questions to ask before any decision, deferring its application to a follow-up post. It is a pragmatic, evidence-leaning stance on school leadership, with a deliberately provocative framing.
points: Leaders with wildly different styles and visible flaws can all run successful schools, which suggests style is not the active ingredient.
Rob Coe's review finds much leadership-style research flawed and its advice not clear, actionable or verified.
What matters is what leaders focus on, such as learning time, supports for students and teachers, and management factors like trust and delivery.
Salles converts the research into fourteen questions a leader can ask before any change.
His own working shortcut is to ask what impact a proposed change will have on progress.
quotes: If you look back over your list, you will probably find this to be true as it is of mine. What made the difference, both good and bad, is what each headteacher did.
We can’t successfully train leaders on the HOW of leadership. There are so many. It is too complex for the leader to pull out the right leadership style at the right time with the right person.
It is much easier, and more streamlined, to train leaders on WHAT they should do.

Much of the plentiful and eagerly attended advice that is given is not clear, actionable or scientifically verified. And the field is riddled with spurious, often implicit, causal claims that are simply not warranted…
Rob Coe also outlines what quality research does say about leadership. It is all about the WHAT - what leaders actually do and focus on.
The time allocated to learning may be thought of as a direct multiplier of the amount of learning that will happen.
